The omission is not doing any rhetorical work here, and because the last item contains its own 'and' ('friends and family'), the series is hard to parse; it reads as if 'talking' were an afterthought or an appositive. A copy editor would add 'and' before the final item. I added it with a serial comma to match the passage's own style elsewhere ('anxiety, depression, and feelings of isolation'). This is the only issue I would mark.

Journalistic prose does this all the time, and the sentence parses cleanly: 'friends and family' is plainly a single unit inside the third gerund phrase. Adding 'and' would be a style choice, not the correction of a definite error. Web search was unavailable, so this verdict does not rely on the original source article.

Supplying the subject explicitly, as the ¶2 fix did ('instead of the plan reining in'), makes the contrast correct: profits go to tax havens instead of being taxed by home governments. 'Their' would be ambiguous here because the nearest plural is 'tax havens', so 'these profits' is the clearer subject.

A to-infinitive ('to serve') is a loose colloquial variant that a careful teacher would correct, and students will memorise this phrase. 'towards' is the minimal fix and suits this British-spelled text; 'to serving' would also be acceptable.

Even so, "go a long way to + infinitive" ("goes a long way to explain/ensure/serve") is a widespread, established variant in edited English, especially British English, where this text sits. The change would be a style preference, not a correction a careful editor must make. Keep the text as it is.

vb.why: Not a definite error.
